items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 26: Obligations of deployers of high-risk AI systems
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, of at least six months
items.why: The binding EU rule and source of the six-month figure. Use in accordance with the instructions for use; input data relevant and sufficiently representative 'to the extent the deployer exercises control' over it; monitoring; suspension and notification where a risk appears; logs kept 'to the extent such logs are under their control' and 'unless provided otherwise' in other law, including data protection law. High-risk systems only. Commission's copy of the consolidated text, stated on the page to be based on the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026, with Digital Omnibus changes marked NEW or AMENDED.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 13: Transparency and provision of information to deployers
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be accompanied by instructions for use
items.why: What the instructions must contain: intended purpose, the level of accuracy to be expected, known circumstances that affect it, human oversight measures and how to collect and interpret logs. Defines the limits inside which the provider's assurances hold. Commission's copy of the consolidated text, stated on the page to be based on the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026, with Digital Omnibus changes marked NEW or AMENDED.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 25: Responsibilities along the AI value chain
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: they modify the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, which has not been classified as high-risk
items.why: The consequence of using a system outside its intended purpose: a deployer whose change makes it high-risk is treated as the provider and takes on the provider's obligations. Commission's copy of the consolidated text, stated on the page to be based on the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026, with Digital Omnibus changes marked NEW or AMENDED.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 113: Entry into force and application
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.locator: Art. 113, third paragraph, point (c)(i), marked AMENDED
items.quote: Chapter III, Sections 1, 2, and 3, with the exception of Article 6(5), shall apply from:
items.why: Source of the date in the brief: Article 26 sits in Chapter III Section 3, which applies from 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for Annex I products. The page footer still says 'Official version of 13 June 2024'; the banner and AMENDED markers were relied on. Commission's copy of the consolidated text, stated on the page to be based on the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026, with Digital Omnibus changes marked NEW or AMENDED.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 99: Penalties
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: obligations of deployers pursuant to Article 26
items.why: Breach of the deployer obligations falls in the tier of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, for an undertaking, up to 3 % of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. Member States set the rules; not used as the brief's figure. Commission's copy of the consolidated text, stated on the page to be based on the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026, with Digital Omnibus changes marked NEW or AMENDED.

items.title: Guidance on AI and data protection: What are the accountability and governance implications of AI?
items.publisher: Information Commissioner's Office
items.quote: you should regularly review any outsourced services and be able to modify them or switch to another provider
items.why: The UK regulator on bought-in AI where personal data is processed: requirements set at procurement, regular review during deployment, and a different solution chosen if compliance cannot be assessed. Guidance, not statute. Marked under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. No date printed; page metadata gives 11 December 2024.

items.title: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Principle 12 'Monitor your system’s behaviour', provisions 12.1-12.4; definition of 'System Operators'
items.quote: System Operators shall log system and user actions to support security compliance, incident investigations, and vulnerability remediation.
items.why: Source of the quotation. The UK government's own statement on logging and monitoring by organisations that deploy AI ('System Operators': any business or organisation responsible for embedding or deploying an AI model and system within its infrastructure). Voluntary, and framed around security, not fairness. Sets no retention period.

items.title: SS1/23 Model risk management principles for banks
items.publisher: Bank of England, Prudential Regulation Authority
items.locator: Principle 2.6 'Use of externally developed models, third-party vendor products', points (a) and (b), PDF p.19
items.quote: validate their own use of vendor products and conduct ongoing monitoring and outcomes analysis of vendor model performance using their own outcomes
items.why: A UK regulator's version of the deployer's duty: responsibility stays with the firm when a model is bought in, vendor data and assumptions are checked, and the firm monitors against its own results. Banks with internal model approval only.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.locator: MANAGE 3.1, Table 4, p.32; MEASURE 2.4, Table 3, p.29; MANAGE 4.1, Table 4, p.33
items.quote: AI risks and benefits from third-party resources are regularly monitored, and risk controls are applied and documented.
items.why: International comparator for monitoring bought-in AI in production and for post-deployment monitoring plans, including override and decommissioning. Voluntary, United States.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in UK financial services - 2024
items.publisher: Bank of England and Financial Conduct Authority
items.quote: 46% of respondent firms reported having only ‘partial understanding’ of the AI technologies they use
items.why: Source of the second figure, and evidence for the gap this question tests: the report attributes partial understanding largely to third-party models. Regulated financial firms only; self-reported; 118 responses.

items.title: Data Protection Act 2018, section 62: Logging
items.publisher: legislation.gov.uk
items.quote: must keep logs for at least the following processing operations in automated processing systems
items.why: A UK statutory logging duty, though not one written for AI: controllers and processors handling personal data for law enforcement purposes must log collection, alteration, consultation, disclosure, combination and erasure, and hand the logs to the regulator on request. Applies only to Part 3 (law enforcement) processing. Amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (words omitted 19 August 2025; 'Commission' substituted 30 September 2026). Sets no retention period.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 5: Principles relating to processing of personal data
items.publisher: legislation.gov.uk
items.quote: every reasonable step must be taken to ensure that personal data that are inaccurate
items.why: The binding UK rule nearest to an input-data check: personal data fed to a system must be accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date, and the controller must be able to show it. Covers personal data only, and is about the data, not the system's outputs.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 12: Record-keeping
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: High-risk AI systems shall technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system.
items.why: The provider-side rule that makes the deployer's log duty possible: a high-risk system must be built to record events, including those relevant to the deployer's monitoring under Article 26(5). A buyer can therefore ask a supplier where the logs are and who holds them. High-risk systems only. Commission's copy of the consolidated text, stated on the page to be based on the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026, with Digital Omnibus changes marked NEW or AMENDED.

items.title: Guidelines for secure AI system development
items.publisher: National Cyber Security Centre, with the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and international partners
items.locator: Section 4 'Secure operation and maintenance': 'Monitor your system's behaviour' and 'Monitor your system's inputs'
items.quote: you monitor and log inputs to your system (such as inference requests, queries or prompts)
items.why: The UK cyber authority on what to watch once a system is live: outputs and performance, so that sudden or gradual change is seen, and inputs, logged for audit and investigation. Written mainly for providers of AI systems, and about security; voluntary. The PDF carries Crown copyright 2023 and no fuller date.

items.title: ETSI TS 104 223 V1.1.1: Securing Artificial Intelligence (SAI); Baseline Cyber Security Requirements for AI Models and Systems
items.publisher: European Telecommunications Standards Institute
items.locator: Clause 5.4.2, Principle 12 'Monitor the system's behaviour', provisions 5.4.2-1 to 5.4.2-4
items.quote: System Operators should analyse their logs to ensure that AI models continue to produce desired outputs
items.why: The UK code of practice quoted in the brief, carried into a published technical specification: organisations that deploy AI ('System Operators') log system and user actions, and should read those logs to catch drift and anomalies. Free to download. A voluntary specification framed around security; sets no retention period.

items.title: Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry: Report, Volume 1 (HC 1119)
items.publisher: Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry (chair: Sir Wyn Williams)
items.quote: the Post Office maintained the fiction that its data was always accurate
items.why: A statutory inquiry's finding on what happens when an organisation treats the output of a bought-in system as beyond question: people in the Post Office knew or should have known the system could err, its data was relied on regardless, and many hundreds were wrongly convicted. Horizon was accounting software, not AI; cited for the deployer's duty to check, not for anything about machine learning. A large file (Volume 1 concerns human impact and redress).

items.title: R (Ayinde) v London Borough of Haringey; Al-Haroun v Qatar National Bank [2025] EWHC 1383 (Admin)
items.publisher: High Court (King's Bench Division, Divisional Court); The National Archives, Find Case Law
items.quote: Freely available generative artificial intelligence tools, trained on a large language model such as ChatGPT are not capable of conducting reliable legal research.
items.why: A UK court on a tool used outside what it can reliably do, with no check on its output: false citations reached the court, and the judges warned of severe sanction for lawyers who use AI for research without verifying it. Concerns lawyers' professional duties; it sets no general rule for deployers.

items.title: WILDS: A Benchmark of in-the-Wild Distribution Shifts
items.publisher: Proceedings of the 38th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 139; P. W. Koh and others
items.quote: On each dataset, we show that standard training yields substantially lower out-of-distribution than in-distribution performance.
items.why: Peer-reviewed evidence for the brief's claim that a supplier's assurances hold only inside the conditions tested: across ten real-world datasets, accuracy fell when a model met data unlike its training data, such as a different hospital. This is the reason for input-data checks and monitoring. A benchmark study of 2021 models; it measures the effect and does not test deployer controls. Only the abstract page was read.

items.title: Reviewable Automated Decision-Making: A Framework for Accountable Algorithmic Systems
items.publisher: arXiv (J. Cobbe, M. S. A. Lee and J. Singh); ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency 2021
items.quote: to provide a systematic framework for determining the contextually appropriate record-keeping mechanisms to facilitate meaningful review
items.why: Peer-reviewed conference paper, read in the authors' repository copy. Argues that record-keeping across the whole decision process, human steps included, is what makes later review and legal challenge possible; explanations of the model alone are not enough. Supports keeping logs and deciding in advance what to log. A framework, not an empirical study. Only the abstract page was read.

items.title: Understanding accountability in algorithmic supply chains
items.publisher: arXiv (J. Cobbe, M. Veale and J. Singh); ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency 2023
items.quote: algorithmic accountability discussions must consider supply chains and the difficult implications they raise for the governance and accountability of algorithmic systems
items.why: Peer-reviewed conference paper by UK authors, read in the authors' repository copy. Explains why the deployer's position is hard: a system bought as a service is produced by several organisations linked by data flows, so no one of them sees or controls the whole. Bears on feeding lessons back to suppliers. Analytical, not empirical. Only the abstract page was read.

items.title: Model Artificial Intelligence Governance Framework, Second Edition
items.publisher: Info-communications Media Development Authority (IMDA) and Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC), Singapore
items.locator: Section 3, 'Operations management': data for model development ('Understanding the lineage of data', 'Ensuring data quality'), p.37-38; paragraph 3.25
items.quote: Organisations are encouraged to understand and address factors that may affect the quality of data
items.why: International comparator on input data: know where data came from and how its accuracy is kept, check accuracy and completeness, and take care with third-party data of mixed origin. Voluntary, Singapore, and dated 2020, before generative AI was in general use.
